definition: Egregious means outstandingly, shockingly bad — a fault or offense so conspicuous it stands out from all the ordinary ones.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word egregious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know egregious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Even the arbitration lawyer winced at the gym contract's egregious fine print, which kept billing members for two full years after they canceled.
Glaring is weaker than egregious: a glaring mistake is merely easy to spot, while an egregious one is shocking in how bad it is, not just in how visible.
Unconscionable goes further than egregious — an egregious foul outrages the crowd, but an unconscionable one leaves the offender with no moral defense at all.

Flagrant is about openness: the offense is committed in plain view, almost defiantly, with no attempt to hide. Egregious ranks the offense itself — how shockingly bad it is — whether or not anyone saw it happen.

Appalling names the reaction — it dismays and horrifies whoever looks at it. Egregious measures the offense against its ordinary kind: this error, this violation, stands out from all the routine ones.

Continuity slips happen in every film, but the courtroom drama's was egregious: the defendant's plaster cast switched arms three times in a single scene, and by the third switch the audience had begun counting aloud.
Ordinary slips escape notice; this one had the whole theater keeping score.
That is the claim egregious makes — not merely that something is wrong, but that its badness stands out from the ordinary run of faults by a margin everyone can see.
Egregious is a ranking word: it does not just call the thing bad, it certifies that the badness stands out from the ordinary run — an egregious error, violation, breach.
The old approving sense ('an egregious talent') is dead; using it as praise today reads as a mistake.
Its near-twin gregarious (met in the root check above) kept the flock's warmth instead.

Inspector Alvarez has written up hundreds of kitchens, and most reports read alike: a propped door, a missing thermometer, a mop in the wrong sink.
Her report on the Harborview Grill is the one her trainees now study, because one violation there was egregious.
For months, the kitchen had been storing raw chicken on the shelf directly above the salad station, drip after drip.
'Ordinary slips are why inspections exist,' she tells trainees.
'This was something else -- a professional kitchen ignoring the first rule everyone learns.' The report's other findings filled two calm paragraphs.
That one got a page, in language nobody would call routine.
